faqs.q: How Many Lessons Will You Actually Need?
faqs.a: This is the honest answer to the question behind the prices. The figure quoted everywhere is around 47 hours of professional tuition plus roughly 20 hours of private practice before test standard. It is a widely repeated industry estimate rather than a figure the DVSA publishes, so treat it as a rough guide. Even as a guide it is useful: at £37 an hour, or £35 within a block, it puts the total well above what most people have in mind when they book a first lesson.

faqs.q: Do Prices Change by Area?
faqs.a: No. A lesson in Canary Wharf costs the same as a lesson in Walthamstow or Barking. The rate is the same across all 51 areas, and pick-up is included wherever you are within them. See the areas we cover for the full list, or ask us if you are just outside one. If you are comparing us with another school, our guide to what moves the price of a driving lesson lists the questions that make two quotes comparable.

faqs.q: Questions?
faqs.a: If something here is not clear, ask before you book rather than after. Read the FAQs → All courses → Full site index →

faqs.q: How much are motorway lessons?
faqs.a: On enquiry. Session length depends on how far you start from motorway-grade road: minutes in Wanstead, a river crossing and a run out to the A2 from Canada Water. Send a postcode and we will quote it.

faqs.q: Can I do this before I pass my test?
faqs.a: Yes, with an approved instructor in a dual-control car showing L plates. Learners have been allowed on motorways since June 2018. It is voluntary and not on the test, so most leave it until after.

faqs.q: Which motorway will I drive?
faqs.a: The M11, joined at junction 4 at Woodford, after a build-up on the A12 and the A406. South of the river, the A2 towards the M25 at Dartford.

faqs.q: Can I book my child's driving test for them?
faqs.a: No. Since 12 May 2026 only the learner can book, change or cancel their own car driving test, and their driving instructor cannot do it for them either. You can still help, as long as your child is with you while you do it, completes as many of the steps as they can, and uses an email address and phone number that are theirs or that they can easily get to. The rules are set out on GOV.UK.

faqs.q: Can I sit in on a lesson?
faqs.a: Yes, if it is arranged in advance, so we can make sure it is safe and practical on the day. Ask when you book. If it cannot be done on a particular lesson, we will tell you plainly rather than leave you guessing.

faqs.q: Will you tell me how my child is getting on?
faqs.a: If they are under 18, yes: we are happy to talk to a parent or guardian about lesson times, pick-up and drop-off points, payment and general progress. Once a learner is 18, their lessons and progress are theirs, so we discuss them with you only if they agree. Our safeguarding policy and privacy policy set out the detail.

faqs.q: I'm paying for my child's lessons. How does that work?
faqs.a: The same way as any booking: cash or bank transfer, as we do not take cards. Single hours are paid at the lesson, and a block of ten hours (£350) or an intensive course is paid before it starts unless we agree otherwise. If your child is under 18, the booking needs your agreement as their parent or guardian, and we are happy to sort out times, pick-up points and payment with you directly.

faqs.q: What payment methods do you accept?
faqs.a: Cash or bank transfer. We do not take cards, so please come to the lesson able to pay one of those two ways. Single hours are settled at the end of the lesson itself. Block bookings, ten hours for £350, and intensive courses are paid before they start, unless we have agreed otherwise.

faqs.q: How much do driving lessons cost?
faqs.a: Automatic lessons are £37 per hour, or £350 for a 10-hour block booking. Refresher lessons are £41 per hour, and the beginner course is taught at the same £37 per hour rate. Intensive courses start at £1,229 for 30 hours and £1,580 for 40 hours. Mock tests, prestige car and motorway lessons are priced on enquiry, and Pass Plus is £260. Call 07706 876263 if you want a quote for a particular course.

faqs.q: What happens if I fail my driving test?
faqs.a: You can book another test straight away, but you cannot sit it until 10 working days have passed. Use them. Your instructor goes through the examiner's marking sheet with you fault by fault, and the next lessons target what actually cost you rather than starting again from the top. If nerves were the problem more than the driving, a mock test, marked the way an examiner marks, is the closest thing to a rehearsal.

faqs.q: Can I use the school's car for my driving test?
faqs.a: Yes, provided you have done your training with us and your instructor is satisfied you are ready to sit it. Test day carries a small extra charge for the car, which we confirm when you arrange it with us. Every service and charge is listed on our prices page. You sit the test in the same dual-controlled automatic you have been learning in, and your instructor takes you to the centre.

faqs.q: Which test centres do you cover?
faqs.a: We cover three test centres in and around East London: Wanstead, Goodmayes and Chingford. The Barking (Tanner Street) centre closed in early January 2026. Your instructor will make sure you get plenty of practice on the exact routes used by your nearest test centre.

faqs.q: How many times can I change my driving test?
faqs.a: Twice. Since 31 March 2026 you can make 2 changes to a car test booking, and changing the date and the centre at the same time counts as one. After that you have to cancel and book again. You make the changes yourself on gov.uk, and to keep your fee you need to give at least 10 full working days' notice: Monday to Saturday count as working days, Sundays and public holidays do not.

faqs.q: How do I know which test centre I'll use?
faqs.a: You choose the centre yourself when you book your practical test on gov.uk. We teach the routes at three centres – Wanstead, Goodmayes and Chingford – and your instructor will suggest one based on where you live and how your driving is coming along, so your later lessons can focus on those roads. Book the centre you actually mean to sit at rather than whichever has the earliest slot: since 9 June 2026 a booked car test can only be moved to one of the 3 test centres nearest it, or back to the one you first booked, and Goodmayes and Chingford are not on each other's list.

faqs.q: How do I book my driving test?
faqs.a: You book it yourself at gov.uk/book-driving-test once you have passed your theory test, using your driving licence number and a debit or credit card. Since 12 May 2026 only the learner can book, change or cancel a car test, and it is against the law for anyone else to book it for you, our instructors included. You can add your instructor's personal reference number when you book so the system checks they are free. The DVSA fee is paid to the DVSA and is not part of any lesson price. Book it once your instructor says you are close to test standard rather than before, and check the waiting time

faqs.q: What is your cancellation policy?
faqs.a: Forty-eight hours' notice to cancel or move a lesson, please. Anything shorter than that, and any lesson simply not turned up to, can be charged at the full rate: your instructor has held the time and cannot usually resell it that late. Real emergencies are treated as real emergencies, so tell us as soon as you know. The full wording is in our terms and conditions.

faqs.q: How long is each lesson?
faqs.a: One or two hours. Two is the better option where it fits your budget and your week: you get more continuous driving, and less of the hour goes on settling in and getting to somewhere useful. Intensive courses work differently, packing the hours into consecutive days rather than spreading them over months.

There is no joining fee, no registration charge and no booking fee. Travel time to reach you is ours to absorb, not yours to pay for.

Ten hours bought together cost £350 rather than £370: £35 an hour, a saving of £20 across the block. That is the only discount we offer, and we would rather state it plainly than dress it up. Blocks are payable in advance.

Most pupils take an hour or two first, decide whether they get on with the instructor, and move onto a block after that. Nobody is asked to buy one on day one, and buying a block does not change what happens in the lesson. When a block is worth it, and when it is not, is set out in our guide to block booking .

That matters most if you are nervous about starting at all. One hour at £37 commits you to nothing else, and it is a small price for finding out whether the thing you have been dreading is as bad as you think. Say so when you book and the hour starts on a quiet street; our guide for nervous learners covers the rest, and the reviews from nervous starters say how it went for pupils who began that way.

An intensive course is a block of tuition compressed into days rather than months, typically around four hours a day over a week to ten days. The 30-hour course starts at £1,229 and suits people with some driving behind them.

The 40-hour course is £1,580 and suits people starting closer to the beginning. Both are taught in the same automatic cars, on the roads around the test centre you have booked, and both are payable in advance unless we agree otherwise.

The course price covers the tuition hours. The DVSA fee for the practical test itself is separate and paid to the DVSA, and using our car on test day carries a small additional charge, confirmed when you arrange it with us. Read the full breakdown on the intensive course page .

A mock test includes the debrief and is priced on request. It runs at the same length as a real test, on a real route around your own centre (Wanstead, Goodmayes or Chingford), and is marked the way an examiner marks. The debrief is the point of it: you leave knowing exactly which faults would have counted and what to do about them.

It is an average, not a target. Some pupils test at 30 hours; others need 60 or more. What moves the number is your starting point, how often you have lessons (weekly beats monthly by a long way), and whether you can practise between them in a car you have access to.

We will tell you where you honestly stand rather than putting you in for a test early, and we would rather you budgeted for the real figure than for a flattering one. More on this in our guide to how many driving lessons you need , and on our pass first time page.

Motorway lessons are priced on enquiry , and the reason is the map: from Leytonstone you are on the M11 in minutes, from Canada Water you cross the river first. Same teaching, different length of session, so we quote from your postcode. Automatic cars, DVSA-approved ADIs, full licence holders and accompanied learners.
Learners could not legally use a motorway in this country until June 2018, and the practical test still does not go near one. So the first motorway most British drivers ever drive, they drive alone.

That is the gap this closes: one road type, taught properly, in a dual-control automatic with a DVSA-approved instructor beside you. There is no office: we collect you anywhere in the 51 areas we cover, seven days a week, 7am to 10pm.

Before June 2018 a provisional licence holder on a motorway was breaking the law. Since then learners have been allowed on, but only with an approved driving instructor, in a dual-control car with L plates showing. It is voluntary, and in practice very few learners take it up before their test.

The test has not changed to match. An examiner will use a dual carriageway if the route has one, and that is as close as it gets. Gantries, all-lane running, a red X, a breakdown with no hard shoulder: none of it is marked, so none of it has to be taught before you pass.
Joining at the speed of the traffic already there, using the whole slip road rather than arriving at the end of it at 45
Lane discipline: left unless overtaking, back to the left once past
Safe gaps: what two seconds looks like at 70, doubled in the wet
Overtaking properly: mirrors, blind spot, decide, go, return
Reading gantries and variable limits early enough to act on them
Smart motorways: all-lane running, the red X, the emergency areas
Leaving early rather than late, off the countdown markers
Breaking down where there is no hard shoulder
Fatigue, and planning the stop before you need it

The red X and breaking down where there is no hard shoulder are the two that catch people out, and we talk both through on the road, long before you could need them. If you would like to read the detail first, it is in our guide to your first motorway drive .

The nearest motorway is the M11, and it starts inside East London: junction 4 at Woodford is the access nearly everyone here uses. It sits at Charlie Brown’s Roundabout, where the A113 Chigwell Road and the A1400 meet beneath the A406 North Circular flyover at the start of the motorway, and the carriageway runs north past Loughton and Epping.

Getting to it is half the teaching. The A12 through Leyton and Leytonstone, and the A406 east from Waterworks Corner, are multi-lane roads with slip roads, and the limit steps up in stages rather than jumping straight to 70. Joining and lane changes get built there, at the speeds those stages allow. For Barking and Newham the A13 does the same job.
South of the river it is the A2, out through Kidbrooke and Bexley towards the M25 at Dartford: a longer run before the first fast mile, which is why there is no single hourly figure here.

An automatic licence is no obstacle, because automatic is all we teach. It also takes a job off the pile at the worst moment: on a short slip road with a lorry closing in lane one there is no gear change to make and nothing to stall.

You must be at least 17 years old to start driving lessons on public roads in the UK. You'll also need a valid provisional driving licence before your first lesson. You can apply for your provisional licence from age 15 years and 9 months.

Yes. You must hold a valid UK provisional driving licence before you can legally drive on public roads. You can apply for your provisional licence online via the DVLA website. It typically arrives within a few days. Once you have it, simply contact us and we'll get you booked in.

Every lesson is taught by a DVSA-approved driving instructor. An ADI has passed three qualifying exams, holds an enhanced DBS check, re-registers with the DVSA every four years and is subject to DVSA standards checks in between. The green badge in the windscreen is the proof, and any instructor should be happy to show you theirs. You can read about the people who teach here on our instructors page .

Longer than most people hope, and the honest answer is that nobody can tell you at the first lesson. The number repeated across the industry is roughly 47 hours of tuition and about 20 hours of private practice, though it is an estimate in wide circulation rather than a published DVSA figure, so use it as a ballpark and nothing firmer.

Your instructor will give you a far more useful read after three or four hours, once they have seen how you handle junctions and traffic. Regular weekly lessons shorten the total; a lesson whenever you remember stretches it.
Yes, and it is all we teach. There is no clutch, no gear stick and nothing to stall, so from the first lesson your attention goes on mirrors, road position and junctions instead of your left foot.

That helps on East London roads, where a lot of the hour is spent stopping and starting behind buses. A licence passed in an automatic lets you drive automatic cars only, which now includes nearly every electric and hybrid on the road.

No. Manual tuition has been discontinued, so every lesson, course and mock test we run is in an automatic car. An automatic licence covers any automatic vehicle, which is most of what is being sold now. If you need a manual licence for a job that requires one, you will need a school that still teaches manual, and we would rather say so before you book than after.

Have your provisional licence on you: you must hold one to drive, and your instructor will ask to see it before you set off. Beyond that, bring nothing. You will not be asked to pull away into traffic: the car is taken somewhere calm first, and only then do you take the wheel.

Expect to spend the hour on getting comfortable at the controls, pulling away, stopping smoothly and looking in the right places at the right time. Most people are actually driving well before the halfway mark. The last few minutes are spent telling you what you did well, what needs work, and what the next hour will cover.

Yes, and it helps to say so when you book, because it changes where your first lesson starts and how quickly it moves. Your instructor collects you and drives somewhere quiet before you swap seats, the car has a second brake on the instructor's side, and with no clutch there is nothing to stall in front of a queue. Nothing is asked of you before it has been explained and shown.

Our guide for nervous learners goes into more detail, and the reviews from nervous starters say how it went for pupils who began the same way. Later on, if it is test nerves that worry you, a mock test on your own centre's routes is the closest thing to a rehearsal.

Book it once your instructor says you are close to test standard rather than before, and check the waiting time when you book: in London it is often long enough that you keep having lessons while you wait. The full steps are in our guide to booking your practical test .

Twice. Since 31 March 2026 you can make 2 changes to a car test booking, and changing the date and the centre at the same time counts as one. After that you have to cancel and book again. Clutch control is where most learners lose their first few hours, and it is what causes stalling at busy junctions. In an automatic there is nothing to stall. Your first hour goes on the mirror-signal-manoeuvre routine, steering and where to place the car, rather than on getting moving at all.

The difference is largest exactly where East London puts you: the stop-start crawl behind buses on a road like Mare Street or Barking Road, where someone learning in a manual is working a clutch every few seconds while you are deciding whether to hold back or go.
Nothing to stall, so a busy junction stops being the thing you dread
Hill starts are the footbrake and nothing else, which matters if you test at Chingford
One pedal to control speed, so more attention left for mirrors, cyclists and signs
Workable for people whose left leg or hip makes a clutch painful or impossible
The same car you are likely to buy: most electric and hybrid cars are automatic
What it does not do is make the test easier. The examiner marks observation, planning and control, and the automatic removes none of that. It removes one distraction from the list.
